podcast.body: This song became the last number one song of the 1970s, hitting the top spot on December 22, 1979, and remaining there for three weeks into the 1980s. Originally titled "Escape," it was renamed due to public demand in record shops. Rupert Holmes wrote the song when he needed an upbeat track to complement an album full of ballads, focusing on lyrics due to the repetitive music. The inspiration came from personal ads in The Village Voice, with Holmes pondering what would happen if he answered one, surmising it would probably be his own wife. His slightly less-than-perfect singing voice was considered crucial to the song's success, making him sound like a relatable character. "The last number one song of the 70s, making it there on December 22nd, 1979, and staying there for three weeks to take us into the 1980s, that song was everywhere."

podcast.body: This song was a huge hit in 1979 and was cited by Jim Stafford as an example of a good novelty song that succeeded due to its musically interesting quality, allowing it to "have legs." "He gave the example of Escape the Pena Colata song by Rupert Holmes a huge hit in 1979."
